items.title: Seoul, South Korea, South Korea: South Korea's KOSPI surged nearly 15% amid a global chip stock rally.
items.description: South Korea's KOSPI surged nearly 15% amid a global chip stock rally.
items.rawSummary: South Korea's stock market, after a 135% surge and a 44% crash erasing $2 trillion, snapped back with a nearly 15% rally on July 31, as the country advances its defense programs and a court sentences former President Yoon to 18 months.
items.analysis: South Korea's equity market has undergone a dramatic cycle: a 135% surge between December and June, powered by chipmakers SK Hynix and Samsung, gave way to a 44% decline over 40 days, erasing roughly $2 trillion in market capitalization. The selloff, amplified by record retail leverage in leveraged ETFs and options, triggered a wave of margin calls; Goldman Sachs reported that more than 1.2 million leveraged retail accounts faced margin calls by July 13, with an estimated 320,000–360,000 fully liquidated, and the tally likely exceeds 500,000 as the KOSPI fell further. Assets under management in leveraged ETFs have dropped 70% from their peak, shedding $37 billion to around $16 billion, the lowest since early April, signaling continued deleveraging. The finance ministry responded with an emergency meeting, imposed around-the-clock market monitoring, restricted leveraged ETF trading, and capped retail exposure, prompting a brief stock rebound. On the morning of July 31, the KOSPI surged nearly 15% amid a rally in global chip stocks, underscoring the extraordinary volatility that now characterizes the market. In separate developments, former President Yoon Seok-yeol was sentenced to 18 months for false campaign statements, while the defense sector advanced: system development of the KF-21 Boramae fighter is complete with mass production set for September, and prototype assembly of the indigenous KSAM-II naval surface-to-air missile has begun.

items.title: Ukraine, Ukraine: Intelligence reports indicated that Russia attacked with North Korean ballistic missiles yesterday, with some striking civilian apartment buildings.
items.description: Intelligence reports indicated that Russia attacked with North Korean ballistic missiles yesterday, with some striking civilian apartment buildings.
items.rawSummary: Combat in Ukraine has seen the emergence of a new short-range air defense system, the loss of a Ukrainian F-16, and a reported missile attack on civilian buildings using North Korean-supplied ballistic missiles.
items.analysis: Video has emerged showing combat use of a Ukraine-operated STASH short-range air defense system against Russian Shahed/Geran-type strike drones. The system integrates US-made AGM-114L Hellfire missiles adapted for anti-aircraft use, an Israeli-origin RADA radar, and a Ford F-350 chassis, and was developed by American defense company V2X. Its first public appearance in Ukraine was in May 2026. Separately, a Ukrainian Air Force F-16 was downed near the frontline; the pilot ejected and was recovered by friendly forces. In the latest reported incident, intelligence reports indicated that Russia used North Korean ballistic missiles in an attack yesterday, some of which struck civilian apartment buildings.

items.title: Beijing, China, China: Reuters detailed that North University of China used Anthropic's Claude 3 Haiku to create synthetic data for a social media monitoring model, and PLA Unit 96941 used OpenAI's GPT-3.5 to summarize military source code, then trained a domestic model on those summaries for use within Chinese military networks.
items.description: Reuters detailed that North University of China used Anthropic's Claude 3 Haiku to create synthetic data for a social media monitoring model, and PLA Unit 96941 used OpenAI's GPT-3.5 to summarize military source code, then trained a domestic model on those summaries for use within Chinese military networks.
items.rawSummary: China denied arms transfer reports to Iran while Reuters detailed how two military-linked Chinese entities used U.S. AI models to build domestic systems for social media monitoring, code summarization, and military network use.
items.analysis: China's Foreign Ministry rejected as not true and not factual reports that Iran will soon receive Chinese-made shoulder-fired air defense missile launchers, with spokesperson Mao Ning stating Beijing works for peace. The denial came after reports of a potential transfer of up to 400 launchers. Separately, Reuters reported that Chinese military-affiliated researchers are leveraging model distillation to train smaller domestic AI systems on outputs from OpenAI and Anthropic models, adapting them for surveillance, cyber warfare, drones, and military targeting. More details emerged later on July 31: North University of China, closely tied to the weapons industry, used Anthropic's Claude 3 Haiku to generate synthetic data for a social media monitoring and content moderation model, while PLA Unit 96941, a military intelligence and cyber-warfare unit in Beijing, employed OpenAI's GPT-3.5 to summarize sensitive military source code and then trained a domestic model on those summaries to operate entirely within Chinese military networks. The practice underscores ongoing efforts to bypass U.S. restrictions on advanced chips and model access while repurposing American AI capabilities for military modernization. The dual developments highlight both diplomatic tensions over arms transfers and the persistent technology race where China draws on foreign AI despite constraints.

items.title: near Kryvyi Rih, Ukraine: President Zelensky states that preliminary findings indicate Russia used a North Korean-supplied ballistic missile in the attack on Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, and says the investigation is ongoing.
items.description: President Zelensky states that preliminary findings indicate Russia used a North Korean-supplied ballistic missile in the attack on Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, and says the investigation is ongoing.
items.rawSummary: A missile strike on a residential building near Kryvyi Rih killed at least six people, with Ukrainian officials and a military source indicating the weapon was likely North Korean, marking the first reported use of such ordnance by Russia in nearly a year.
items.analysis: A Ukrainian military source told Reuters that the missile was North Korean-manufactured, marking the first time Russia has used such a weapon in almost twelve months. President Zelensky later said the preliminary assessment also identified a North Korean ballistic missile, calling for further investigation and highlighting the alliance's role in killing Ukrainian civilians. The reintroduction suggests Moscow may be turning again to Pyongyang's stockpiles as its own missile production strains under wartime demand. The attack on a civilian building underscores the continued danger to non-combatants far from front lines. Military-technical cooperation between Russia and North Korea could expand further amid Western sanctions pressure.

The Pentagon awarded Lockheed Martin a $58.6 billion Patriot interceptor contract extending through 2032, with analysts warning that ongoing fighting in Iran and Ukraine is drawing down American high-end air defense inventories to levels that will take years to replenish; separately, Trump told the Financial Times he is “not sure” about licensing Ukraine to produce Patriot missiles, contrasting with earlier signals of approval. On the economic front, core PCE inflation remained at 3.3%, nearly double the Federal Reserve’s target, while Senate Democrats highlighted that the reassignment of DHS personnel to immigration enforcement has left 300 intelligence vacancies and no new election-security staff ahead of the November 2026 midterms. President Trump also publicly clashed with Republican senators over his attorney general nominee, threatening to temporarily withdraw the nomination, and Treasury Secretary Bessent held a high-level call with China’s Vice Premier He Lifeng to prepare for President Xi’s expected September visit amid ongoing technology and Iran tensions.

items.title: Parchin Military Complex, near Tehran, Iran: The Telegraph reported that the U.S. and Israel are considering a land blockade of Iran to increase economic pressure, a plan that would involve neighboring countries restricting border crossings to limit Iran's imports and exports.
items.description: The Telegraph reported that the U.S. and Israel are considering a land blockade of Iran to increase economic pressure, a plan that would involve neighboring countries restricting border crossings to limit Iran's imports and exports.
items.rawSummary: U.S. airstrikes across multiple Iranian provinces continue, the hunt for the hidden supreme leader intensifies, and the U.S. and Israel are now reported to be weighing a land blockade to tighten economic pressure.
items.analysis: The Parchin military complex near Tehran has been under scrutiny as U.S. operations in Iran expand, though no strikes on the capital region were initially noted and it remains unclear whether Parchin itself has been targeted. CENTCOM confirmed two waves of airstrikes on dozens of IRGC military targets overnight and through the morning of July 30, releasing footage of the operations. The Times reported that the CIA and Mossad are intensifying the search for Ayatollah Mojtaba Khamenei, who has not been seen publicly since a February 2026 airstrike and is believed to be hiding underground near Tehran or Qom. In a separate development on July 31, The Telegraph detailed that U.S. and Israeli officials are considering a land blockade of Iran, aiming to persuade neighboring countries to restrict border crossings and strangle Iran’s economy after military action failed to force negotiations. The feasibility of such a blockade is in doubt given Iran’s extensive borders, but the discussion signals a search for non-kinetic leverage alongside the ongoing bombing campaign.
